newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Serbs vow not to hand over war criminals to U.N..
newsitem.headline: Serbs vow not to hand over war criminals to U.N..

text.p: In a challenge to the new U.N. secretary-general, the Bosnians Serbs vowed not to hand over their leaders for trial to the U.N. war crimes tribunal, warning that such action could provoke violence and warfare.

Professor Biljana Plavsic, president of the Bosnian Serb republic, in a Jan. 2 letter to Secretary-General Kofi Annan, said he should be aware that the Bosnian Serbs would not hand over Dr. Radovan Karadzic, their former president, and military commander Gen. Ratko Mladic, the two most prominent suspects indicted by the Hague-based tribunal.
The letter was obtained by Reuters on Thursday.

Wishing Annan success in his new post, Plavsic said that the indictments were no longer valid and that any arrest of the two men would "threaten the existing peace" and rekindle "massive civil and military unrest."

"The present position of the Republika Srpska is that we are unwilling to hand over Dr. Karadzic and Gen. Mladic for trial in the Hague as we believe that any such trial now falls outside of the scope of the tribunal's constitutional framework," she said.

The letter, with an accompanying three-page statement, is expected to be discussed by the Security Council. One Western diplomat said that while it was a repetition of previous positions, its declarative manner was "very worrying."

Plavsic said that legally the Security Council was empowered to deal with only peace and security and had created the tribunal because it believed war crimes were a threat to peace. Now that fighting was over, she argued, the council could no longer press the indictments.

"Whether or not the reports mentioned were true and accurate at the time, we do not believe that there are now any reports of mass killings, systematic detention, rape of women and ethnic cleansing," she said.

"In the opinion of the authorities of the authorities of the Republika Srpska and as far as the Bosnian Serbs are concerned, there is no longer any threat to peace," she said. "To this extent, therefore, the constitutional basis for establishing the tribunal (has) disappeared."

"This leaves the question of whether the trials of Dr. Karadzic and Gen. Mladic in particular are required for the maintenance of peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina," she said. "We think that the answer to this question is clearly in the negative."
Plavsic said that if the two men were to be handed over, such action would "in fact threaten the existing peace.
"We believe that massive civil and military unrest would result in the Republika Srpska which might well prove uncontrollable by the civil authorities.

"The chances of fighting re-starting would, in our judgment be high," she said. "These would be even higher were any attempt made to hunt down Dr. Karadiz and Gen. Mladic and forcibly bring them to trial."
She said neither man held public office any longer, "nor is it our intention that they shouold do so in the future."

NATO troops in Bosnia have a mandate to arrest the two men if its soldiers encounter them during the course of duty. But commanders on the ground have avoided going out of their way to hunt them down.
Plavsic also contended that neither man could get a fair trial because of the "overwelming and worldwide level of adverse publicity" given to them.

"This perception applies equally to the judges of the tribunal," she said, including President Antonio Cassese, who had wanted the September Bosnian elections postponed until the two had been arrested.
